Remove detections that imply an impossible speed

Source: R/filter_speed.R
filter_speed.Rd

Orders each animal's detections in time and computes the straight-line speed between consecutive detections from the positions of the receivers' deployments. A step is a violation when the receivers are more than min_dist_m apart and the speed exceeds max_speed_ms, or when two receivers that far apart log the animal at the same moment; receivers closer than min_dist_m can both hear one position, so steps between them are never violations.

Usage

filter_speed(
  x,
  max_speed_ms,
  min_dist_m,
  support_s = 3600,
  reference_tags = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A detset().

max_speed_ms

Highest plausible speed, metres per second.

min_dist_m

Receivers closer than this, in metres, are never a violation: the largest distance at which two receivers can hear one transmission.

support_s

Half-width, in seconds, of the window that counts each endpoint's supporting detections. It decides which endpoint of a violation goes. Which steps are violations does not depend on it.

reference_tags

Optional data frame with a transmitter column. Pairs of stations that heard one transmission of these tags are never a violation.

Value

x with the detections kept and one log record (reasons spike

and weaker_endpoint). Detections with no animal_id or no deployment position are kept and counted in the record, with the station pairs the reference tags cleared.

Details

min_dist_m is therefore the largest distance at which two receivers of the array can hear one transmission, and it has no default: set too low, the filter removes true detections of one transmission heard at two receivers seconds apart. In a large lake array, reference tags can be heard by stations more than 3 km apart within 5 s, and a min_dist_m below that distance removes detections of one transmission heard at two stations. reference_tags adds what the reference tags show: two stations that heard one transmission of a reference tag within the codetect_s of check_settings() (5 s) can both hear one position, whatever their distance, so steps between them are never violations.

The filter works in passes. A detection whose steps in and out are both violations is a spike and goes first. Spikes can sit next to each other: in A B A B A, with a false B on each side of a true A, that A is a spike too. In each run of adjacent spikes, only the spikes with the fewest supporting detections go in a pass, and the next pass tests the rest again. When no spike remains, each violating step loses its weaker endpoint: the one with fewer detections of the same animal within support_s seconds at receivers within min_dist_m. A tie removes the later endpoint. The passes repeat until no violation remains, at most 100 times.

Steps of zero time between distant receivers are violations. As the endpoint with less support goes, one false first detection removes itself and leaves the run of true detections after it.

Detections with no animal_id take no part. When no detection of x has an animal_id, the filter removes nothing and says so in a message.

See also

Other filters: filter_animals(), filter_deployment_period(), filter_duplicates(), filter_min_detections(), filter_min_lag(), filter_post_release(), filter_release(), filter_tag_life(), minimum_lags()

Examples

study <- detqc_example
dets <- detset(study$detections, study$deployments, study$animals)
dets <- filter_speed(dets, max_speed_ms = 3, min_dist_m = 2000)
writeLines(strwrap(detset_log(dets)$reason[2], width = 72))
#> removed 0 of 3,297 detections (0%); 0 animals lost every detection; 0
#> passes; 0 detections with no animal or position kept; 0 station pairs
#> cleared by reference tags
